Raising in a Regulated Category

Analysislowob research

By lowob · 11 June 2026 · Updated 16 November 2026 · 7-minute read · Strategy

Fintech investors underwrite trust and durability, not growth alone. Show the licence as an asset, the economics per funded account, the losses and the compliance cost in the model, and the plan for when a partner leaves. Two recent events sharpen every one of those questions: the 2024 bankruptcy of the banking-as-a-service provider Synapse, which led the FDIC to propose new recordkeeping rules for fintech custodial accounts, and a run of 2026 US charter approvals that gave some fintechs a path to holding the customer relationship themselves.

This is operating guidance from go-to-market work, not investment, legal or regulatory advice.

Licensing is an asset: price it like one

Most decks bury licensing in "regulatory" on the risks slide. Move it to the assets slide.

A granted licence tells an investor three things. The regulator looked at you and said yes. You can operate without borrowing someone else's permission. And the next competitor needs the same months and the same spend to catch up.

The months are real and measurable. Davis Wright Tremaine's August 2026 review of OCC approvals traced one de novo national bank from application on 18 December 2025 to conditional OCC approval on 8 May 2026 and FDIC deposit insurance approval on 4 August 2026. Circle's national trust bank received conditional approval in December 2025 and final approval on 10 July 2026. The same review notes the OCC said in June 2026 that filings must be complete at submission and that it may return materially deficient ones. In the UK, the FCA reported that 97.9% of authorisation cases were decided within their deadline from April to June 2026, but that new firm authorisations and payment services and e-money authorisations both missed their targets.

A licence in progress is still an asset if you show the path: the application date, the stage, the known gaps, the budget, the fallback if it slips. Raise against evidence, not narrative said raise on evidence. A dated application with a named responsible person is evidence.

What you cannot do is leave it vague. "We are exploring licensing options" reads as "we have not started."

Licence statusWhat to showWhat it signals
GrantedLicence, scope, conditions, supervisorPermission to operate in your own name
FiledFiling date, stage, open questions, budgetA path with a timeline an investor can test
PlannedTarget regime, adviser, filing date, costIntent; fundable only with a partner in place
Not needed yetThe partner whose licence you use, and whyDependency, which the partner slide must answer

The unit is a funded account

Sign-ups are not the unit in fintech. Downloads are not the unit. A verified account with no money in it is a cost, not a customer.

Build the unit economics around the funded account: cost to acquire one, cost to verify and onboard one, revenue per funded account per month, and how long a funded account stays funded. Then the payback period on that basis.

Investors who know the category will convert your sign-up numbers to funded accounts in their heads anyway. Do it for them and show the ratio. A low ratio with a clear plan beats a hidden ratio every time. From funded account to lifetime value covers the full calculation.

Compliance and losses belong in the model

Two lines fintech models often leave out: the cost of compliance and the cost of losses.

Compliance cost is people, tooling, audits, legal, and the verification spend per account. It scales with accounts and with the number of markets. Put it in as its own line so an investor can see it does not eat the margin at scale.

Losses are fraud, chargebacks, credit losses if you lend, and operational errors. Show the rate, the trend, and what you changed when it moved. A loss rate that fell after a control change is a strong slide. A loss rate that is absent is a question you will get asked in a worse setting.

The partner bank question

If you run on a partner bank or a BaaS provider, every experienced fintech investor will ask the same question. What happens if they give notice?

The question has a recent history. Synapse Financial Technologies, a banking-as-a-service intermediary, went bankrupt in April 2024. In September 2024 the FDIC proposed recordkeeping and reconciliation requirements for banks holding custodial deposit accounts with transactional features, which Sullivan & Cromwell described as a response to that bankruptcy and as requiring significant changes to the account structures many banks and fintechs use. We could not confirm whether a final rule has been issued. Separately, the 2023 interagency guidance from the OCC, the Federal Reserve and the FDIC sets out how banks must manage third-party relationships across their life cycle, scaled to how critical the activity is. Your partner bank is applying that guidance to you.

They are not asking whether you have a dependency. Almost everyone does. They are asking whether you understand it. The answers they want:

What they askWhat a good answer contains
Who is the partner?Named, with the agreement term and notice period
What do they control?Account issuance, custody, card programme, compliance sign-off, or all of it
What do they cost?Fees in the model, including minimums and step-ups
What is concentrated?Share of revenue or accounts running through that partner
Who holds the ledger?Where the record of each customer's balance lives, and how often it is reconciled with the bank
What is the exit plan?Second partner in diligence, or a licence path that removes the dependency, with a timeline

A one-slide version of this table does more for the round than another slide on market size.

Investors find the uncomfortable items anyway. Finding them in your room says you run the company; finding them elsewhere says you hide things.

The fintech data room

Run the round like a sales process said build the data room before the first meeting. In fintech the room has a specific extra shelf.

Licences and registrations, current and in progress. The compliance programme: policies, the named compliance officer, the monitoring approach, the last audit or review and what it found. Bank partner and BaaS agreements. Ledger reconciliation reports. Any external audit or attestation. Loss data by month with the control changes marked. Complaint volumes and resolution times. Regulatory correspondence, including anything uncomfortable.

The uncomfortable items go in on purpose. Investors find them anyway. Our Build Order for financial services and fintech covers how to keep these records as a matter of routine, so the room is an export rather than a project.

Strategic investors want distribution or data

Banks, payment networks and large payroll or accounting platforms invest in fintech for reasons that are not purely financial. Usually they want one of three things: distribution into your customers, data on a segment they cannot see, or an option to acquire you later.

None of these is bad. All of them change the deal. A strategic investor can bring a partnership that cuts your acquisition cost in half. They can also bring exclusivity terms that close off the other channels in Distribution when the platforms are closed. PitchBook's midyear 2026 outlook noted that public-market favour was going to sectors with regulatory support, naming fintech and crypto among them, which makes the "option to acquire" conversation more likely to come up.

Decide what you want from them before the meeting. Then ask directly what they want from you. The answer tells you whether the cheque is worth the terms.

lowob takeaways

  • Move licensing to the assets slide. Show status, dates, budget and a responsible person.
  • Build economics per funded account. State the sign-up to funded ratio before an investor works it out.
  • Give compliance cost and losses their own lines. Show the trends and the control changes.
  • Answer the partner bank question on one slide. Include who holds the ledger and the exit plan.

Common questions

What do fintech investors look for in a pitch?

Trust and durability, not growth alone: licensing shown as an asset, economics per funded account, compliance cost and losses in the model, and a plan if a partner bank leaves.

How should a fintech startup answer the partner bank question from investors?

Name the partner with the agreement term and notice period, what they control and cost, how concentrated you are, who holds the ledger, and the exit plan: a second partner in diligence or a licence path, with a timeline.

How long does it take a fintech to get a US bank charter?

It varies. One 2026 de novo national bank went from application in December 2025 to conditional OCC approval in May 2026 and FDIC approval in August 2026, and conditional approval still has to be followed by final approval.

What should be in a fintech data room?

Licences and registrations, the compliance programme, bank partner and BaaS agreements, ledger reconciliation reports, audits or attestations, monthly loss data with control changes marked, complaint data and regulatory correspondence.
